# The Graph Engineering Revolution in AI: DeerFlow 2.0, Claude Code and the End of Isolated Agents!

The video explains the difference between loop engineering, in which an agent decides his own path, and graph engineering, in which the paths and passages of work are defined in the code. Then shows how DeerFlow 2.0 applies this with subagents, on-demand skills and a sandbox for agents to work.

Video by Maurício Yokoyama Issei, published on August 12, 2026 (9 min 16 s).
Watch: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dacWmQubuSs

_The video and the transcript are in Portuguese. The minutes between brackets, such as [04:12], point to the excerpt of the video._

## From chat to stream automation

The AI agents ceased to be chat assistants and began to automate complex workflows [00:00]. For this to work without the system hallucinating or locking, the software design had to change [00:00].

## Loop Engineering

The problem is to make AI solve complex tasks without losing control of the process [01:04]. When a single agent does a long task from beginning to end, the chance of him getting lost is great [01:04].

In loop engineering, a single agent runs a continuous cycle until the problem is solved. Whoever develops defines the goal, and the path stays with the agent [01:24]. The cycle usually has five steps: finding out what you need, planning, performing, checking your own work and correcting [01:47]. If wrong, the agent restarts the cycle alone [02:10].

## Graph Engineering: the organogram

The video uses an analogy: the loop is a generalist professional who tries to solve everything on his own; the graph is the organization chart of a company, in which those who develop define the paths and passages of responsibility [02:30].

A graph has three parts [02:50]:

- **We:** the experts, who perform the work [02:50].
- **Edges:** they say where the work goes afterwards, in sequence or in parallel [02:50].
- **Shared status:** the collective memory of the system [03:12].

## When to use each

If the task is linear and has a clear end, the loop suffices [03:32]. If it is necessary to divide the task, rotate parts in parallel and pass the work in a formal way, the graph is better [03:32]. In the graph, each node can use a different model and tool, and a failure is isolated [03:53].

The rule is to dominate the loop first. The graph is an architecture pattern, not a magic solution: use it only when control and parallelism justify [03:53]. The starting point should be the simple and cheaper loop [04:15].

## DeerFlow 2.0

According to the video, DeerFlow has almost 80,000 stars in GitHub [04:37]. Version 2 ranked first on GitHub Trending on February 28, 2026, and the tool went from deep research to orchestration platform [04:57].

DeerFlow does not depend on a template: you can use DeepSeek, OpenAI or Gemini [05:17]. It is open source, with MIT license, integrates with Slack and Telegram and can be extended by MCP protocol [05:39].

## Subagents and skills

The lead agent acts like a manager. It creates subagents on demand, but only when there is clear gain, how to rotate actions in parallel or isolate the context [06:00].

Skills are gradually loaded, only when they are requested, which keeps the context clean and saves tokens [06:22]. Already come skills for deep search, code, slides, web pages, images and videos [06:43]. As are Markdown files, any skill can be created or exchanged [07:03].

## A computer for agents

DeerFlow gives agents an isolated sandbox, which can run in a Docker container or Kubernetes [07:24]. There the agent has browser, terminal and real files, and can work for hours without leaving isolation [07:24].

The agent reads files, runs commands in the shell, tests the code that wrote and corrects errors [07:44]. There is also integration with Claude Code in the terminal to send tasks and accompany the subagents [08:05].

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Should I start with a loop or a graph?

With a loop. The graph is only worth it when the task calls for control and parallelism [04:15].

### Does DeerFlow force you to use a specific model?

Nope. It works with various suppliers such as DeepSeek, OpenAI and Gemini [05:17].

## About the video

In this video, we dive deep into the future of artificial intelligence architecture and the historical transition that is happening in the developer community: the evolution of Loop Engineering to Graph Engineering.
If you have already frustrated yourself with autonomous agents who "lose their course" in long tasks or want to understand how to build predictable and scalable multiagent systems, this content is indispensable.
We explore DeerFlow 2.0, ByteDance's powerful open source framework for deep-search and coding long-term tasks
, and we analyze the innovative deer-workflow pilot project (DeerWork), which establishes the basis for the DeerFlow 3.0, bringing orchestration entirely to TypeScript and delegating semantic work to replaceable agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pi.
What you will learn in this video:
Loop vs. Graph Engineering: Discover the fundamental difference between leaving an agent free to choose your own path in a loop or declaring explicit paths, edges and checks using agent graphs.
The Metaphor of the Organogram: Because agents are no longer "generalists" who do everything themselves to work on structures with defined roles and data hands-offs.
DeerFlow 2.0 Anatomy: The role of sandboxes Safe Docker, short-term persistent memory and integrated message gateways with Telegram, Slack and Lark
.
Dynamic Workflow Runtime: How to use TypeScript as the deterministic execution plan of your system, using primitive flow as parallel(), pipeline() and phase().
Orchestration of Replaceable Agents: Like Claude Code, Codex and Pi act as plugable and modular semantic gears under a unified and neutral supplier interface.
